name: System-Level Eval
question: Did the agent get the job done?
summary: Treat the agent as a black box. Give it a real task, let it run to completion, and check only the final result against the goal. This is the number stakeholders care about, and the one to gate releases on.
useCases: Release gates and regression checks before shipping a new prompt, model or tool
Comparing two agent versions on the same task set
Tasks with a checkable end state: tests pass, a record is updated, a file exists

items.detail: share of tasks solved in all k repeated trials
p50 / p95 wall-clock time per task
turns taken; flags loops and waste

steps: Build a golden set of 50–200 realistic tasks, each with a verifiable end state
Write programmatic checkers for each end state wherever possible
Run every task several times, because agents are non-deterministic
Report success, pass^k, cost and latency together, never success alone
pitfalls: A pass says nothing about why. Pair it with process-level eval to debug
One lucky run hides flakiness, so use repeated trials
String-match checkers reject correct answers that are phrased differently
remember: Score the outcome, count the cost, repeat the run.
caption: Only the final state is checked. What happened inside the agent is out of scope.

code.text: by_task = {t.id: [r["ok"] for r in results if r["task"] == t.id] for t in TASKS}
pass_k = sum(all(v) for v in by_task.values()) / len(TASKS)
cost_per_success = sum(r["cost"] for r in results) / max(sum(ok), 1)
p95 = statistics.quantiles([r["secs"] for r in results], n=20)[18]

steps.title: Build a golden set
steps.text: Collect 50–200 real tasks. Each needs an end state that code can check: a database row, a file, a passing test.

steps.title: Run every task several times
steps.text: Agents are non-deterministic, so run each task K times (3–5 is typical). Record cost and wall-clock time for every run.

steps.title: Check the end state, not the wording
steps.text: A checker function inspects the final state. Two runs pass; one leaves the order in the wrong status and fails.

steps.title: Aggregate the metrics
steps.text: Success rate averages all runs. pass^k counts tasks that passed every run. Add cost per success and p95 latency.

steps.title: Gate the release
steps.text: Ship only if every threshold holds. Here success is 0.87, below 0.90, so this version is blocked.

pros: Measures what users and stakeholders actually care about
Simple to explain and to automate as a release gate
Works with any agent framework: only the end state matters
Catches regressions in cost and latency as well as quality
cons: Says nothing about why a run failed
Needs tasks with an end state code can check
Flaky unless each task runs several times
A lucky path can hide unsafe or wasteful intermediate steps
avoidWhen: You need to debug one specific failure (use process-level eval)
Outputs are open-ended with no checkable end state (use LLM-as-a-Judge)

playgroundGuide.scenario: You own the release of a customer-support agent. Before shipping, you replayed 5 real support tasks, 3 times each: 15 runs in total. Each cell below is one run. ✓ means the agent reached the correct end state (for example, the order status was right); ✗ means it didn't.
controls: Click any cell to flip that run between pass (✓) and fail (✗).
Drag the slider to set what one run costs in model tokens.
Or pick a ready-made scenario to see a typical pattern.

outputs.name: Success rate
outputs.meaning: Passing runs ÷ all 15 runs. Your average quality.

outputs.name: pass@3
outputs.meaning: Tasks that passed at least once ÷ 5. Can the agent do it at all?

outputs.name: pass^3
outputs.meaning: Tasks that passed all three runs ÷ 5. Can you rely on it every time?

outputs.name: Cost per success
outputs.meaning: Total spend ÷ passing runs. What each good outcome really costs.

outputs.name: Release gate
outputs.meaning: Ships only if the success rate is at least 90%.

presets.name: Starting data
presets.expect: A realistic mix: 73% success, the gate blocks the release.

presets.name: Reliable agent
presets.expect: 14 of 15 runs pass. Expect 93% success, pass^3 of 80%, and the gate passes.

presets.name: Flaky agent
presets.expect: Every task fails exactly once. Expect pass@3 of 100% but pass^3 of 0%: it can do everything, but never reliably.

presets.name: One broken task
presets.expect: Task 4 always fails, the rest always pass. Expect 80% on every metric: consistent, with one capability gap to fix.

missions.text: Make the release gate pass by flipping as few cells as possible.
missions.hint: The gate needs 90% of 15 runs, so at least 14 must pass.

missions.text: Get pass@3 to 100% while pass^3 stays at 0%.
missions.hint: Every task must pass at least once and fail at least once.

missions.text: With the cost slider at $0.05, push cost per success above $0.10.
missions.hint: The spend stays at $0.75, so you need fewer than 8 passing runs.

tools.type: Open source · UK AI Security Institute
tools.best: Rigorous, reproducible evaluations of agents that use tools, written in Python and run from the command line.
tools.ex: Run 150 support tasks for 5 epochs against two model versions and compare accuracy and token use in the log viewer.
pros: Repeated epochs, sandboxes and tool-using agents built in
Detailed log viewer for every sample
cons: More concepts to learn than a YAML test runner
No hosted team dashboard out of the box

tools.best: Declarative test suites in YAML that run in CI and fail the build when quality drops.
tools.ex: A GitHub Action that blocks a pull request if a prompt change drops the pass rate on 100 test cases below 90%.
pros: Fast to start; simple suites need no code
Side-by-side comparison of prompts and models
cons: Complex agent flows need custom providers
Very large suites get unwieldy in YAML

tools.best: Pytest-style unit tests for LLM apps, with many ready-made metrics including task completion.
tools.ex: A test file that runs on every commit and fails if task-completion scores on your golden set fall below 0.8.
pros: Large metric library, including agent metrics
cons: Scores depend on the judge model you configure
Team dashboards need the paid platform

tools.best: Hosted datasets, experiments and regression comparison, connected to full traces.
tools.ex: Compare version 12 and version 13 of an agent on the same dataset, then open each failing run’s trace.
pros: Traces and evaluations in one place
cons: Smoothest with LangChain and LangGraph, though it works with any stack

tools.best: Experiment tracking with strong diffing, so a team can see exactly which cases improved or regressed.
tools.ex: Every prompt change runs as an experiment; the diff view lists the 7 tickets that newly fail.

tools.best: Learning from a registry of example evals and simple templates.
tools.ex: Read how exact-match and model-graded evals are structured before designing your own suite.
cons: Less actively developed than newer frameworks

goals: Explain the difference between success rate, pass@k and pass^k
Calculate pass^k and cost per success from raw run results
Design a release gate with thresholds for quality, cost and latency

practice.scenario: A stockbroker's support agent answers “Why was my order rejected?”. Before every release, 150 recorded cases are replayed five times each. A run counts as a success only if the agent names the correct rejection reason from the order log. The release ships only if success stays at or above 90% and p95 latency stays under 8 seconds.

industries.use: Gate releases of order-status and KYC assistants on replayed real tickets
Track refund-agent resolution rate and cost per resolved ticket
Measure plan-change agents on completion rate across repeated runs

practice.analogy: A driving test. The examiner checks whether you parked safely in the bay and on time, not how you held the steering wheel.

library.name: Inspect AI
library.what: Open-source eval framework from the UK AI Security Institute. Datasets, solvers and scorers in plain Python, with repeated trials (epochs) built in.

samples.code:
from inspect_ai import Task, task
from inspect_ai.dataset import Sample
from inspect_ai.scorer import includes
from inspect_ai.solver import generate

@task
def order_rejections():
    return Task(
        dataset=[
            Sample(input="Why was order 8812 rejected?",
                   target="INSUFFICIENT_MARGIN"),
            Sample(input="Why was order 9034 rejected?",
                   target="PRICE_BAND_BREACH"),
        ],
        solver=[generate()],   # swap in your agent (tools + loop)
        scorer=includes(),     # success = target reason appears in the answer
        epochs=5,              # repeat each case: agents are non-deterministic
    )

inspect eval task.py --model openai/gpt-4o-mini
inspect view      # browse accuracy, per-sample runs, tokens and time

numericDrill.question: You ran 4 tasks × 3 trials. T1 ✓✓✓, T2 ✓✗✓, T3 ✓✓✓, T4 ✗✗✓. What is pass^3?
numericDrill.answer: Success rate over all runs = 9 of 12 = 75%. pass^3 counts tasks that passed all 3 trials: T1 and T3, so 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5. The gap between 75% and 0.5 is flakiness.

interview.question: Why isn't a single success-rate number enough for an agent release gate?
interview.answer: Agents are non-deterministic and cost money per run. Report success over repeated trials (pass^k for consistency), cost per success and p95 latency. A new version can keep the same success rate while doubling cost or becoming flaky.

interview.question: How do you build a golden task set for system-level eval?
interview.answer: Sample real, anonymized requests across intents and difficulty, add known edge cases and past failures, and give each task a programmatically checkable end state such as a database row, a file or a passing test. Keep 50–200 tasks, version the set, and add every new production failure to it.

mistakes.mistake: Grading only the final message with string matching
mistakes.fix: Check the end state in code: the order status, the file, the test result
Run 3–5 trials and report pass^k alongside the average

quiz.question: Your order-status agent resolves 47 of 50 replayed tickets on a single run. The support head wants to ship on Friday. What do you do first?
options: Ship it: 94% beats the 90% target
Replay each ticket 3–5 times and gate on pass^k
Add 50 more tickets and run them once
Switch to a larger model
quiz.explanation: One run can pass by luck. Repeating each ticket shows which ones work every time, which is what customers experience.

quiz.question: A refund agent says “Your refund is done.” Which checks prove the refund really happened? Select all that apply.
options: The order status in the database is “refunded”
The refunded amount in the payments table matches the policy
The reply contains the word “refunded”
An audit-log entry exists for the refund
quiz.explanation: End-state checks inspect real systems. The reply can say “refunded” when nothing happened.

quiz.question: A rebooking agent is replayed 3 times on 3 disruption cases. Case A passes 3/3, B passes 2/3, C passes 0/3. What is pass^3?
quiz.explanation: pass^3 counts a case only if all three runs passed. Only A did: 1 ÷ 3 ≈ 0.33.

quiz.question: Same results (A 3/3, B 2/3, C 0/3). The product manager puts pass@3 in the release note. What number is that, and what is the problem?
options: 0.67, but it counts cases that passed at least once, while each customer gets one run
0.33, and it is the right number to publish
1.0, because every case was attempted
0.56, the average across runs
quiz.explanation: pass@3 = 2 ÷ 3 ≈ 0.67. It is optimistic: a customer gets one attempt, not the best of three.

quiz.question: You are writing the release gate for a plan-change agent. What belongs in it? Select all that apply.
options: Success rate over repeated trials
Cost per successful task
p95 latency
Number of lines in the system prompt
quiz.explanation: Gate on what customers and the business feel: quality, cost and speed.

quiz.question: Version 2 of a claims agent keeps 92% success, but cost per successful claim rises from $0.04 to $0.11. What does this show?
options: Ship it: quality held
A cost regression the gate should catch
Nothing: cost is not part of evaluation
Only process-level eval matters here
quiz.explanation: Nearly 3× the cost for the same quality is a regression. Put cost in the gate.

quiz.question: You are building the golden set for an appointment-booking agent. Where should the tasks come from?
options: Tasks the team imagines
Real, anonymized patient requests plus past failures
Only the easiest cases
A public benchmark
quiz.explanation: Real traffic and known failures make the set representative of what the agent will face.

quiz.question: A dispute agent passes 95% of golden tasks, yet operations found it opened duplicate dispute tickets in 4% of runs that still ended “resolved”. Why did the gate miss it?
options: It checked only the final status, not side effects along the way
pass^k was set too low
The judge was biased
The benchmark was contaminated
quiz.explanation: Outcome checks miss harmful steps. Add a “no duplicate tickets” end-state check and score the trace with process-level eval.

quiz.question: Why run golden tasks against a sandboxed copy of production data?
options: So checkers can inspect realistic end states without touching real customers
To make the agent faster
Because string matching requires it
It is not necessary
quiz.explanation: You need realistic state to check, without real money moving or real customers affected.

quiz.question: The same checkout-help task passes on some runs and fails on others, and the failing runs are the ones where the sandbox payment API happened to be slow. What kind of problem is this?
options: A capability gap
Flakiness caused by the environment
Judge bias
Benchmark contamination
quiz.explanation: It works sometimes and fails sometimes depending on conditions. That is flakiness, and repeated trials expose it.

quiz.question: Your KYC agent’s test suite was written six months ago. Live complaints are about cases the suite never covered. What is the fix?
options: Keep the suite frozen so scores stay comparable
Add recent complaint cases to the golden set and keep growing it as a regression set
Raise the pass threshold
Test only with a public benchmark
quiz.explanation: A golden set is a living asset. Every production failure should become a new test case.

quiz.question: The checker for a password-reset task passes if the reply contains “reset link sent”. What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing: it is a clear check
It passes even if no email was sent; check the email outbox or audit record instead
It should check for “password” too
It should use an LLM judge
quiz.explanation: Check the state change (an email queued for that user), not what the agent says it did.

quiz.question: A delivery-query agent averages 4 s per answer, but p95 is 19 s. The goal is that 95% of customers get an answer within 10 s. Does it pass?
options: Yes: the average is well under 10 s
No: p95 is 19 s, so more than 5% of customers wait over 10 s
Yes, if the success rate is high
You cannot tell without pass@k
quiz.explanation: Averages hide the slow tail. Gate on the percentile the goal is written in.

quiz.question: A prior-authorization agent has pass^1 = 0.90 and pass^5 = 0.62. What does that tell you?
options: It is reliable
Many tasks succeed only some of the time, so it has a consistency problem
pass^5 is always lower, so ignore it
The golden set is too small
quiz.explanation: If every task passed 90% of runs, pass^5 would be about 0.9⁵ ≈ 0.59. So failures are spread across many tasks: reliability, not capability, is the problem.

quiz.question: Two prompt versions score 88% and 90% on a 50-task set, one run each. Can you say version 2 is better?
options: Yes: 2 points is a clear win
No: 2 points is one task, which is within run-to-run noise; add trials or tasks
Yes, if the model is the same
No: prompts cannot be compared
quiz.explanation: On 50 tasks, one task is 2 points. Repeat the runs or enlarge the set before declaring a winner.

quiz.question: A claims agent made 200 runs with 150 successes, and total spend was $30. What is the cost per successful task?
quiz.explanation: Divide spend by successes, not runs: $30 ÷ 150 = $0.20.

quiz.question: In a sandbox run, the agent books the right hotel but charges the customer’s card twice. How should the checker score the run?
options: Pass: the hotel is booked
Fail: the correct end state includes exactly one charge
Partial credit
Ignore it: sandbox charges are not real
quiz.explanation: The end state is everything that changed. A double charge is a failed task.

quiz.question: When should the full golden-set eval run for a tutoring agent? Select all that apply.
options: On every prompt, model or tool change before release
On a schedule, to catch drift
Only once, at launch
When the provider updates the model version
quiz.explanation: Anything that changes behaviour, including silent provider updates, should trigger the eval.

quiz.question: After launch, which production signal best stands in for system-level success on a support agent?
options: The ticket is not reopened within 7 days
Number of messages in the chat
Average reply length
Total thumbs-up count
quiz.explanation: Reopen rate tracks whether the problem was actually solved. Thumbs-up ratings are sparse and biased.

quiz.question: A new model scores 3 points higher on your golden set, but p95 latency goes from 6 s to 14 s. The gate is 8 s. What is the decision?
options: Ship it: quality went up
Block the release: every gate condition must pass
Average quality and latency
Remove latency from the gate
quiz.explanation: A gate is several conditions, and all must pass. Tune the setup or route traffic before shipping.
